mainTopic: The מלאכה of כותב (writing) on שבת: what counts as liable writing, which materials and surfaces qualify, and which cases are exempt
overview: The משנה sets the basic rule for the מלאכה of כותב on שבת: writing two letters in one הֶעְלֵם makes a person חייב. It lists inks and surfaces that count, rules on writing on or scratching into the skin, and gives a long list of exempt cases. These include writing that does not last, writing in an unusual way, writing that is not a new two-letter text, and letters that are not read together. The גמרא defines the five inks and explains that 'anything that makes a mark' covers every lasting material valid for a גט. It brings רבי אליעזר's proof about scratching on skin from בן סטדא, which the חכמים reject, followed by a short side discussion about that name. It then shows that two exempt cases in the משנה go against רבי אליעזר and רבי יהודה. It also discusses a single letter that completes a ספר, and רבי אמי's ruling that letters written in two cities make one חייב. The amud ends with a ברייתא about correcting one letter, explained by רב ששת and רבא, and opens a new ברייתא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Writing two letters makes one liable, and the inks that count
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that writing two letters in one הֶעְלֵם is a חיוב on שבת. It lists inks that qualify, plus any substance that leaves a mark.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone who writes two letters during one lapse of awareness is liable. This applies if he wrote with דְּיוֹ, סַם, סִיקְרָא, קוֹמוֹס, or קַנְקַנְתּוֹם, or with anything that leaves a mark.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens the chapter with the basic measure for the מלאכה of כותב: two letters. It then lists the kinds of ink that count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The minimum amount for liability is two letters, not one. The material only needs to leave a lasting mark. The five named inks are examples, and the phrase 'anything that leaves a mark' widens the list. The גמרא will define each ink and explain what that last phrase adds.

keyTerms.meaning: One lapse of awareness (a single unknowing act, for a חטאת)

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule of 'two letters' and 'a lasting mark' is the foundation for every case that follows in the chapter.

phrases.english: MISHNAH

phrases.aramaic: הַכּוֹתֵב שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת בְּהֶעְלֵם אֶחָד — חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: One who writes two letters in one lapse of awareness is liable.
If he wrote with deyo, with sam, with sikra,
with gum, or with copper sulfate,
or with any substance that makes a mark.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַכּוֹתֵב שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת בְּהֶעְלֵם אֶחָד חַיָּיב
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing two letters in one הֶעְלֵם, with any marking substance, makes one חייב.

steps.title: Letters on two surfaces that are read together
steps.stepSummary: Two letters written on two corner walls, or on two leaves of a writing tablet, still make one חייב if they are read together.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote on two walls that meet at a corner, or on two leaves of a writing tablet, and they are read together, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds that the two letters do not have to be on one surface. What matters is that a reader sees them together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the two letters form one readable unit. Corner walls and the leaves of a פִּנְקָס sit side by side, so the eye reads the letters as one piece of writing.
steps.confusionAlert: Remember this case. Later in the משנה, two walls of a house and two leaves of a פִּנְקָס that are NOT read together are פטור. The difference is only whether the letters are read together.

phrases.english: On two walls forming a corner
or on two leaves of a writing tablet,

phrases.aramaic: וְהֵן נֶהֱגִין זֶה עִם זֶה — חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and they are read together, he is liable.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Letters on separate surfaces count together if they are read together.

steps.title: Writing on skin versus scratching into skin
steps.stepSummary: Writing on one's skin makes one חייב. For scratching letters into the skin, רבי אליעזר holds one is חייב a חטאת, and the חכמים hold one is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who writes on his flesh is liable. One who scratches letters into his flesh: רבי אליעזר makes him liable for a חטאת, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה rules on writing on the human body. It then brings a מחלוקת about cutting letters into the skin without ink.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing with ink on skin is ordinary writing on a surface. Scratching adds no ink; it only makes a mark by cutting. רבי אליעזר treats that mark as writing. The חכמים do not treat it as the real מלאכה.

keyTerms.meaning: Sin-offering brought for an unintentional sin

phrases.english: One who writes on his flesh is liable.
One who scratches letters on his flesh:
Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable to a sin-offering,
and the Sages exempt him.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing on skin is חייב. Scratching into skin is a מחלוקת between רבי אליעזר and the חכמים.

steps.title: Writing that does not last is exempt
steps.stepSummary: Writing with liquids, fruit juice, road dust, or scribes' dust, or any material that does not last, is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote with liquids or fruit juice, with road dust or scribes' dust, or with anything that does not last, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now turns to the exempt cases. It starts with materials whose writing fades or blows away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors step 1. There, anything that leaves a mark is חייב. Here, anything that does not endure is פטור. A מלאכה on שבת must produce a lasting result.

phrases.english: If he wrote with liquids, with fruit juice,
with road dust, with scribes' dust,
or with any substance that does not endure, he is exempt.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing that does not last is פטור.

steps.title: Unusual manner, incomplete writing, and letters not read together
steps.stepSummary: Several cases are פטור. These include writing in an unusual way, writing only one letter next to existing writing, tracing over writing, splitting a ח into two ז, letters on ground and rafter, and letters on surfaces not read together.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote with the back of his hand, with his foot, his mouth, or his elbow; wrote one letter next to existing writing; wrote over writing; meant to write a ח but wrote two ז; wrote one letter on the ground and one on a rafter; or wrote on two walls of a house or two leaves of a tablet that are not read together, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists a group of exempt cases. In each one, something about the writing is not normal or not complete.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing with the foot, mouth, or elbow is not the normal way to write (כלאחר יד). A single letter, or tracing over existing letters, is not a full new two-letter text. Letters that are not read together, like ground and rafter or walls that do not meet, do not form one piece of writing.

keyTerms.meaning: With the back of his hand (an unusual way of writing)

phrases.english: With the back of his hand, with his foot, with his mouth, or with his elbow;
if he wrote one letter adjacent to existing writing;
or writing over writing;
if he meant to write a chet
and wrote two zayins;
one letter on the ground and one on a rafter;
if he wrote on two walls of a house,
or on two leaves of a writing tablet

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין נֶהֱגִין זֶה עִם זֶה — פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and they are not read together, he is exempt.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing in an unusual manner, writing that is not a complete new two-letter text, and letters not read together are all פטור.

steps.title: A single letter used as an abbreviation
steps.stepSummary: Writing one letter that stands for a whole word (נוטריקון) is a מחלוקת. רבי יהושע בן בתירא holds one is חייב, and the חכמים hold one is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote one letter as an abbreviation, רבי יהושע בן בתירא makes him liable and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes with a מחלוקת about whether one letter that carries the meaning of a word counts as enough writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the minimum is two letters. רבי יהושע בן בתירא looks at the meaning: a letter that stands for a full word counts as writing. The חכמים keep the strict rule of two actual letters.

keyTerms.meaning: An abbreviation; a letter standing for a whole word

steps.whatToRemember: In the משנה, liability needs two letters, written in the normal way, in a lasting material, and read together. Each exempt case is missing one of these conditions.

phrases.english: If he wrote one letter as an abbreviation:
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira deems him liable,
and the Sages exempt him.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether a single abbreviating letter counts is a מחלוקת between רבי יהושע בן בתירא and the חכמים.

steps.title: Defining the five inks in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the Aramaic name for each ink in the משנה. רבה בר בר חנה identifies סיקרא, and in the name of שמואל identifies קנקנתום as cobblers' black.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: דְּיוֹ is soot-ink. סַם is arsenic dye. סִקְרָא, said רבה בר בר חנה, is called red paint. קוֹמוֹס is gum. קַנְקַנְתּוֹם, said רבה בר בר חנה in the name of שמואל, is the black that cobblers use.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by explaining what each unfamiliar ink in the משנה actually is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a definition step, not an argument. The משנה used Hebrew names, and the גמרא translates them into the everyday Aramaic of its time. This tells the learner which real substances are meant.

phrases.english: GEMARA
Deyo is deyota (soot ink).
Sam is samma (arsenic dye).

phrases.aramaic: סִקְרָא — אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה:
phrases.english: Sikra: Rabba bar bar Chana said:
Its name is sikreta (red paint).
Komos is koma (gum).

phrases.aramaic: קַנְקַנְתּוֹם — אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Kankantom: Rabba bar bar Chana said that Shmuel said:
It is the black of the cobblers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the inks listed in the opening line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each named ink is identified with a known substance.

steps.title: What does 'any substance that makes a mark' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the phrase from the משנה and asks what extra case it comes to include.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And with any substance that makes a mark': what does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's general phrase and asks what it adds. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already listed five inks, so a general phrase seems to need a purpose. The גמרא assumes the extra words must include materials that were not covered by the list.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it come to include?

phrases.english: 'And with any substance that makes a mark.'
What does it come to include?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defining the named inks to the general phrase that follows them.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which additional materials are included by the general phrase 'anything that makes a mark'.

steps.title: It includes fruit juice and gallnut juice, which are valid for a גט
steps.stepSummary: The phrase includes the teaching of רבי חנניא: a גט written with טריא juice or gallnut juice is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include what רבי חנניא taught: if one wrote it (a גט) with the juice of טַרְיָא or with gallnut juice, it is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The extra phrase includes materials that count as real writing for a גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא borrows from the laws of גיטין. If a material is lasting enough to make a valid גט, it is also real writing for שבת. So writing with these juices on שבת is חייב.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse this with step 4. There 'fruit juice' was פטור. The juices here are special kinds that leave a lasting mark.

phrases.english: To include that which Rabbi Chananya taught:
If he wrote it with teriya juice or gallnut juice, it is valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase includes lasting materials like טריא juice and gallnut juice, which are valid for a גט.

steps.title: Also included: lead, soot, and shoeblack
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא from רבי חייא adds that a גט written with lead, soot, or shoeblack is valid. So these also count as writing for שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא taught: if one wrote it with lead, with soot, or with shoeblack, it is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second source listing more materials covered by 'anything that makes a mark'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds to the answer in step 9 using the same logic. A material that makes a valid, lasting גט is also writing on שבת. The list now includes metals and black pigments.
steps.whatToRemember: 'Anything that makes a mark' covers every lasting material that would be valid for writing a גט. Writing with any of these on שבת is חייב.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya taught:
If he wrote it with lead, with soot, or with shoeblack, it is valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a parallel ברייתא to the answer of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Lead, soot, and shoeblack are also included as lasting writing materials.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר's proof that scratching on skin counts as writing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of scratching on one's skin. A ברייתא then shows רבי אליעזר proving it is real writing from בן סטדא, who carried spells out of מצרים scratched on his skin.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one who scratches letters on his skin. A ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר said to the חכמים, didn't בן סטדא take magic spells out of מצרים by scratching them on his skin?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's case of scratching letters on skin. It brings a ברייתא where רבי אליעזר offers a proof that this is a real form of writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי אליעזר holds a person is חייב for scratching letters on his skin, and the חכמים hold he is פטור. His proof is that someone once used skin-scratching as a real way to record and carry information. That suggests people do treat it as writing.

keyTerms.meaning: one who scratches or cuts marks

phrases.english: One who scratches letters on his flesh.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר לָהֶן רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר לַחֲכָמִים:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer said to the Sages:

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲלֹא בֶּן סָטָדָא הוֹצִיא כְּשָׁפִים מִמִּצְרַיִם
phrases.english: Didn't Ben Stada take magic spells out of Egypt
in a scratch that was on his flesh?

steps.triggerLanguage: וַהֲלֹא בֶּן סָטָדָא הוֹצִיא כְּשָׁפִים מִמִּצְרַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case in the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אליעזר's view that scratching on skin is real writing and makes one חייב
steps.raayaSupportSource: The incident of בן סטדא recording spells on his skin

steps.title: The Sages reject the proof because he was a fool
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer that בן סטדא was a שוטה. We do not learn normal behavior from an abnormal person.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: he was a fool, and one does not bring proof from fools.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים push back on רבי אליעזר's proof. They say his example is not a valid source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability for writing on שבת depends on what normal people do. One odd person writing on his skin does not make skin-scratching a normal way of writing, so the proof falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: a fool, a person who does not act normally

steps.whatToRemember: The מחלוקת stays: רבי אליעזר says skin-scratching is writing, and the חכמים say it is not normal writing, so one is פטור.

phrases.english: They said to him: He was a fool,
and one does not bring proof from fools.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof, not רבי אליעזר's whole position.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The source is an abnormal person, and an abnormal person's behavior cannot define normal writing.

steps.title: Side question: why is he called בן סטדא?
steps.stepSummary: As a side point, the גמרא asks why the ברייתא calls him בן סטדא when he was known as בן פנדירא.
steps.simpleTranslation: "בן סטדא"? He was בן פנדירא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the שבת topic for a moment to clear up a name. This question sets up a short back-and-forth about that name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The halachic discussion is finished. This is only a digression to explain why the person in the ברייתא has two different names.

keyTerms.meaning: another name given for the same person

steps.confusionAlert: This short section, ending at step 18, has nothing to do with the laws of שבת. It only explains a name.

phrases.english: "Ben Stada"? He was the son of Pandeira!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side question about a name mentioned in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why he is called by two different names

steps.title: רב חסדא: one name is the husband, the other is the father
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא explains that סטדא was the mother's husband and פנדירא was the man who actually fathered him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: the husband was סטדא, the one who had relations with her was פנדירא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the name question. He says each name comes from a different man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two names do not contradict each other. One comes from the man known as his father, and the other from his biological father.

keyTerms.meaning: the man who had relations with her

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
The husband was "Stada"; the one who had relations with her was "Pandeira."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: סטדא was the husband's name, and פנדירא was the biological father's name.

steps.title: But the husband was פפוס בן יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא: the mother's husband is known to have been פפוס בן יהודה, not סטדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Was the husband not פפוס בן יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא's answer. It points out that the husband had a different, known name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the husband was פפוס בן יהודה, then סטדא cannot be the husband's name. So רב חסדא's explanation does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: the name given for the mother's husband

phrases.english: Was the husband not Pappos ben Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's claim that סטדא was the husband
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The husband's known name was פפוס בן יהודה, so סטדא cannot be his name.

steps.title: Rather, סטדא was his mother's name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the explanation: סטדא was his mother's name, and he was called after her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, his mother was "סטדא."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. It says the name סטדא came from his mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the husband's name was פפוס, the name בן סטדא must refer to the mother, and he was named for her.

phrases.english: Rather, his mother was "Stada."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer of step 14 after the challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-assigns the name to a different person

steps.title: But his mother's name was מרים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: his mother is known as מרים, a women's hairdresser, not סטדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Was his mother not מרים, the braider of women's hair?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new answer. It says the mother also had a different name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the mother's real name was מרים, then סטדא is not her actual name either. This explanation now seems to fail too.

phrases.aramaic: אִמּוֹ מִרְיָם מְגַדְּלָא שְׂעַר נְשַׁיָּא הֲוַאי?
phrases.english: Was his mother not Miriam, the braider of women's hair?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִמּוֹ מִרְיָם מְגַדְּלָא שְׂעַר נְשַׁיָּא הֲוַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that סטדא was the mother's name

steps.title: סטדא was a nickname, as they say in פומבדיתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves it: סטדא was not her real name but a nickname, from the Aramaic סטת דא, "this one strayed from her husband."
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, as they say in פומבדיתא: "This one strayed from her husband."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final answer to the name question. סטדא was a nickname, not a real name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her real name was מרים. סטדא is a play on words meaning "she strayed," a nickname that described her conduct. This ends the side discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: פומבדיתא, a major Torah center in בבל

phrases.english: Rather, as they say in Pumbedita:
This one strayed from her husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17 and closes the side discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reads the name as a descriptive nickname
steps.terutzMaskana: סטדא is a nickname meaning "she strayed."

steps.title: Who taught that one letter next to writing is exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: one who writes a single letter next to existing writing is פטור. It asks which תנא holds this.
steps.simpleTranslation: "He wrote one letter next to writing." Who is the תנא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה. It asks whose opinion stands behind the ruling that one letter next to existing writing is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding one letter next to existing writing might seem to complete something meaningful. So the גמרא wants to know who does not count that small addition.

keyTerms.meaning: who is the תנא (whose opinion is this)?

phrases.english: He wrote one letter next to existing writing.
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה, which rules him פטור.

phrases.english: Who is the Tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side discussion to the next case in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא rules that one letter next to writing is פטור

steps.title: Not רבי אליעזר, who counts even one thread
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב הונא says the משנה does not follow רבי אליעזר. רבי אליעזר holds that adding even one thread to woven cloth makes one חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב הונא said: not like רבי אליעזר, for if it were רבי אליעזר, he said one thread onto woven cloth is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב הונא answers the question. He says the משנה must go against רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר holds that a tiny addition to an existing item counts, as with one thread added to woven cloth. By that logic, one letter added to existing writing should also make one חייב. Since the משנה says פטור, it does not follow him.

keyTerms.meaning: not in line with the opinion of

phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Huna said:
It is not like Rabbi Eliezer,
for if it were Rabbi Eliezer, didn't he say:
One thread onto woven fabric makes one liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא: דְּלָא כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה does not follow רבי אליעזר, who holds that a small addition to an existing item makes one חייב.

steps.title: Who taught that writing over writing is exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: one who writes over existing writing is פטור. It asks which תנא holds this.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Writing on top of writing." Who is the תנא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the משנה. It asks whose view says that tracing over existing letters is not writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether going over letters that already exist creates anything new. The גמרא looks for the תנא who says it does not.

keyTerms.meaning: writing on top of existing writing

phrases.english: Writing on top of writing.
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה, which rules him פטור.

phrases.english: Who is the Tanna?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּתָב עַל גַּבֵּי כְּתָב מַאן תַּנָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same type of question as step 19, asked about a new case in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא rules that writing over writing is פטור

steps.title: Not רבי יהודה, who lets one sanctify God's name by tracing over it
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the משנה does not follow רבי יהודה. He proves this from a ברייתא: a סופר meant to write the name יהודה, left out the ד, and ended up writing שם השם without the right intent. רבי יהודה says he traces over it with his pen while intending holiness. The חכמים say such a שם is not ideal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: not like רבי יהודה. As taught: if someone needed to write God's name, but intended to write "יהודה" and mistakenly left out the ד, he passes a quill over it and sanctifies it, says רבי יהודה. The חכמים say: the name is not of the best quality.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question. He uses a ברייתא to show that רבי יהודה treats writing over writing as real writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה lets the סופר trace over the letters with proper intent, which means he sees tracing as a new act of writing. If so, he would make one חייב for writing over writing on שבת. The משנה says פטור, so it follows the חכמים, who do not see tracing as truly writing anew.

keyTerms.meaning: he sanctifies it, writes it with holy intent

steps.confusionAlert: Without the ד, the name יהודה turns into God's four-letter name. That is why the סופר has accidentally written שם השם.
steps.whatToRemember: Two cases in the משנה are traced to a תנא by showing whom they argue with: one letter next to writing is not like רבי אליעזר, and writing over writing is not like רבי יהודה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: דְּלָא כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: It is not like Rabbi Yehuda.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה צָרִיךְ לִכְתּוֹב אֶת הַשֵּׁם,
phrases.english: As it was taught: If someone needed to write the Divine Name,
but intended to write "Yehuda,"
and he erred and did not put the dalet in it,
he passes a quill over it and sanctifies it.
These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

phrases.aramaic: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵין הַשֵּׁם מִן הַמּוּבְחָר.
phrases.english: And the Sages say: The name is not of the ideal quality.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: דְּלָא כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה does not follow רבי יהודה, who treats tracing over letters as real writing.

steps.title: ברייתא: one letter or one thread that completes the whole item makes one liable
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that writing one letter that completes a ספר, or weaving one thread that completes a garment, makes one חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught: if he wrote one letter and completed a book, or wove one thread and completed a garment, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a single small act. Here, that act finishes a whole item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally one letter or one thread is too small to make one חייב. But when it completes the whole item, the ברייתא says one is חייב. This seems to clash with the משנה's ruling that one letter is פטור, which sets up the next question.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא: כָּתַב אוֹת אַחַת וְהִשְׁלִימָהּ לְסֵפֶר,
phrases.english: It was taught: If he wrote one letter and with it completed a book,

phrases.aramaic: אָרַג חוּט אֶחָד וְהִשְׁלִימוֹ לְבֶגֶד — חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: or wove one thread and with it completed a garment, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: כָּתַב אוֹת אַחַת וְהִשְׁלִימָהּ לְסֵפֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new source on single-letter writing, related to step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One letter or thread that completes a whole item makes one חייב.

steps.title: Who is the Tanna of this ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose opinion the ברייתא follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is the תנא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whose view this ברייתא follows. This sets up two possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה rules that one letter is פטור, the גמרא needs to know who would make one חייב for a single letter or thread.

phrases.english: Who is the Tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the source of the ברייתא in step 23.

steps.title: רבא בר רב הונא: it is רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב הונא says the ברייתא follows רבי אליעזר, who makes one חייב even for one thread added to woven cloth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב הונא said: it is רבי אליעזר, who said one thread onto woven cloth is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב הונא answers that this ברייתא follows רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits what he said in step 20. רבי אליעזר counts a small addition to an existing item, so for him one letter or thread is enough to make one חייב. The משנה follows the רבנן instead.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הִיא,
phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Huna said: It is Rabbi Eliezer,
who said: One thread onto woven fabric makes one liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the question in step 24.

steps.title: רב אשי: even the רבנן agree when it completes the item
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the ברייתא can follow the רבנן too, because finishing a whole item is a different case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: You can even say it is the רבנן; completing is different.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different answer. He says even the רבנן, who usually make one פטור for one letter, agree here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן make one פטור for a lone letter that is just added. But a letter or thread that finishes the whole item is a significant act of completion, so one is חייב. One explanation is that he is at least חייב for מכה בפטיש, the final step that completes a vessel.

keyTerms.meaning: you can even say it follows the רבנן
the final finishing blow, completing an item

steps.whatToRemember: One letter is usually פטור according to the רבנן. But רב אשי holds that if that letter finishes the whole ספר, even the רבנן make one חייב, because completing an item is a significant act.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general idea in הלכות שבת: an act that finishes an item can be significant even when the act itself is tiny.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבָּנַן,
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: You can even say it is the Rabbis;
completing an item is different.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative to רבא בר רב הונא's answer in step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא can follow the רבנן, because completing an item is a special case that makes one חייב.

steps.title: Two letters written in two different cities
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי rules that if one writes one letter in טבריא and another in ציפורי, he is חייב. It counts as real writing, and the letters are only missing closeness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said: If someone wrote one letter in טבריא and one letter in ציפורי, he is חייב. It is real writing; it is only missing being close together.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי gives a new ruling. Two letters written far apart, even in different cities, still count as writing two letters on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that one becomes חייב for writing two letters. רבי אמי says distance does not cancel the writing. The two pieces can simply be carried together, so the only thing missing is closeness, not a real act.

keyTerms.meaning: טבריא, a city in the גליל
ציפורי, another city in the גליל

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said:
If one wrote one letter in Tiberias
and one in Tzippori, he is liable,
since it is writing; it is only lacking closeness.
phrases.notes: Once the two pieces are brought together, they read as two letters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic within the laws of writing: letters written far apart from each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two letters written in different cities make one חייב, because the writing is complete and only closeness is missing.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה about two walls and two tablet pages
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אמי from a משנה. Letters written on two walls of a house, or on two pages of a tablet that are not read together, make one פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in a משנה: If someone wrote on two walls of a house, or on two pages of a writing tablet, and they are not read together, he is פטור!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי אמי's ruling with a משנה. That משנה says letters written apart from each other make one פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two walls of one house, or two pages of one tablet, are much closer than two cities. If the משנה exempts those cases, it seems it should surely exempt writing in two cities. So רבי אמי's ruling looks wrong.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn in a mishna:
If one wrote on two walls of the house
or on two pages of a writing tablet

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין נֶהֱגִין זֶה עִם זֶה — פָּטוּר!
phrases.english: and they are not read together, he is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אמי's ruling in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's ruling that letters written in two cities make one חייב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If letters on two nearby walls or tablet pages make one פטור, then letters in two distant cities should make one פטור even more.

steps.title: The difference: needing an extra act to join the letters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in the משנה's case, an extra act is needed to bring the letters together. In רבי אמי's case, no extra act is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, in the משנה, an extra act is needed to bring the letters together. Here, no extra act is needed to bring them together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי אמי by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Distance is not what matters. What matters is whether you must do something to the object itself, like cutting the wall or the tablet, before the letters can sit side by side. Separate papers in two cities can just be carried together, so nothing is truly missing.

keyTerms.meaning: An act needed to bring them together

steps.whatToRemember: Letters written apart count together if nothing has to be done to the object itself to join them, no matter how far apart they are.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think distance decides the case. Two cities are farther apart than two walls, yet the cities make one חייב. The test is whether an extra act, like cutting, is needed.

phrases.english: There, an act of bringing them together is lacking,
phrases.notes: The wall or tablet would need to be cut or torn to put the letters side by side.

phrases.english: here, an act of bringing them together is not lacking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28 by telling the two cases apart.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Distance between letters decides whether they count together, so the משנה should exempt two cities as well.
steps.terutzMaskana: The test is whether an extra physical act is needed to join the letters. Separate papers need none, so רבי אמי's ruling stands.

steps.title: A ברייתא: fixing one letter makes one liable
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one who corrects a single letter on שבת is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught: If someone corrected one letter, he is חייב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It says correcting just one letter makes a person חייב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is surprising, because writing needs two letters to make one חייב. The גמרא is about to question it.

phrases.english: A tanna taught: If one corrected one letter, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: correcting a letter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Correcting one letter on שבת makes one חייב.

steps.title: How can fixing one letter be worse than writing one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: writing a whole letter makes one פטור, so how can merely correcting one letter make one חייב?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, if someone wrote one full letter he is פטור. Could it be that if he corrected one letter he is חייב?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא with a simple logical problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing one full letter is a bigger act than fixing one letter. If the bigger act makes one פטור, the smaller act should too. So the ברייתא seems not to make sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Now (introduces a 'how much more so' style argument)

phrases.english: Now, if one wrote one letter he is exempt,
yet if he corrected one letter he is liable?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא in step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that correcting one letter makes one חייב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Writing a full letter, which is a bigger act, makes one פטור, so a smaller correction should not make one חייב.

steps.title: רב ששת: turning a ח into two ז's
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא is talking about someone who removed the roof of a ח and turned it into two ז's.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: What case are we dealing with here? Someone who removed the roof of a ח and made it into two ז's.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the challenge by placing the ברייתא in a specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The letter ח looks like two ז's joined by a roof on top. Removing the roof creates two separate letters at once. So this person really produced two letters, which is the normal amount for being חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here? (narrows a source to a specific case)
Its roof (the top line of the letter)

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
With what are we dealing here?
For example, where he removed the roof of a chet
and made it into two zayins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 31.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא makes one חייב for producing just one letter.
steps.terutzMaskana: The correction actually produces two letters, so the normal two-letter rule applies.

steps.title: רבא: turning a ד into a ר
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a different case: someone removed the small corner of a ד and turned it into a ר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: For example, someone who removed the corner of a ד and made it into a ר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers another answer. He says the ברייתא works even when only one letter is changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here no two letters are made, only one. One explanation is that the person is חייב for completing the text, under the מלאכה of מכה בפטיש, the finishing blow. So רבא understands that fixing a letter can be a different kind of liability than writing two letters.

keyTerms.meaning: Its corner or small point (the bump at the back of the ד)
The final hammer blow, the מלאכה of finishing an item

steps.whyThisMatters: רבא's answer shows that the ברייתא may not depend on the two-letter rule at all. Fixing a text can count as finishing it.

phrases.english: Rava said:
For example, where he removed the corner of a dalet
and made it into a reish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the challenge of step 31, instead of רב ששת's answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a correction that produces two letters, like רב ששת's case, could make one חייב.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even changing a single letter makes one חייב, because the correction completes the text (מכה בפטיש).

steps.title: A new ברייתא begins: intending to write one letter
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא starts with the case of someone who intended to write one letter. The rest continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught: If someone intended to write one letter...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move by starting a new ברייתא. Its ruling comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא is about what the person intended, in contrast to what he actually wrote. Hold this opening in mind until the ruling arrives.

phrases.english: A tanna taught: If one intended to write one letter
phrases.notes: The ברייתא continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new ברייתא about intention while writing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup only; the ruling about intending to write one letter follows on the next amud.
